title: Business Organization & Environment Adventure 3: Ansoff & Scales of Operation
welcome_lead: Today you'll plot growth on the Ansoff matrix and weigh economies vs diseconomies of scale.
meta_desc: IBDP Business Management: Ansoff growth matrix and economies/diseconomies of scale.
final_note: You used Ansoff to classify four growth strategies and identified internal economies and diseconomies of scale.

concepts.def: New product in new market — highest risk
Falling unit cost as output rises
Rising unit cost from coordination failure

walkthroughs.body_html:
Ansoff (1957) crossed product with market.

- Penetration: sell more of the same to the same buyers — lowest risk.
- Market development: same product, new region or segment.
- Product development: new product, same buyers.
- Diversification: new product AND new market — highest risk and reward.

As output rises, unit cost falls because fixed costs spread and inputs become cheaper.

Internal sources: technical (bigger machines), purchasing (bulk discounts), managerial (specialists), financial (cheaper loans), marketing (national ads spread thin).

External sources: industry clusters, shared infrastructure.

Beyond a point, unit costs rise again.

Causes: communication breakdown in tall hierarchies, worker alienation, coordination cost, duplication.

The U-shaped long-run cost curve identifies the minimum efficient scale — the smallest output at which average cost is minimised.
